notes.meaning: Jeroboam's son Abijah became very sick. Even kings and royal families face pain and illness in life. This sickness came as a warning from God after Jeroboam led the people into false worship.

Jeroboam told his wife to put on a disguise and travel to Shiloh to see the prophet Ahijah. Ahijah was the prophet who had first promised Jeroboam that he would become king. Jeroboam knew his golden calf idols could not help him, but he was ashamed to seek God openly.

The king told his wife to take a simple present of bread, cakes, and honey to the prophet. In those days, people often brought a small gift when asking a prophet for guidance. The plain food helped her look like an ordinary country woman instead of a queen.

The queen obeyed her husband and traveled to Ahijah's home in Shiloh. Ahijah was an old man by this time and could no longer see with his eyes. Even though his physical sight was gone, God still spoke directly to his heart.

Before the queen arrived, the Lord spoke to Ahijah and told him she was coming. God revealed that she was asking about her sick son and that she would be wearing a disguise. God gave the prophet the exact words he needed to say.

As soon as Ahijah heard her footsteps at the door, he called her by name and asked why she was pretending to be someone else. He told her immediately that he had painful news from God. No human trick can ever hide the truth from the Lord.

Ahijah gave the queen a message to take back to Jeroboam. The Lord reminded Jeroboam that He had taken him from an ordinary background and made him a ruler over Israel. God had given him great honor and authority.

God had torn ten tribes away from the royal line of David to place them in Jeroboam's care. Yet Jeroboam refused to follow the example of King David, who loved God and obeyed His laws. When David sinned, he repented, but Jeroboam stubbornly turned away from the Lord.

The prophet declared that Jeroboam had done worse evil than all the rulers before him. He made golden calves and other metal idols to lead the nation into false worship. By doing this, he treated the living God with utter contempt.

God declared that He would bring total ruin on Jeroboam's family. Every male in his royal household, whether slave or free, would be destroyed. The Lord would wipe away his dynasty just as completely as someone sweeps away trash or dung.

Ahijah warned that family members who died in the city would be eaten by wild dogs, and those who died in the countryside would be eaten by vultures. To lie unburied was considered a terrifying disgrace in the ancient world. This severe judgment showed how serious their rebellion was.

The prophet told the queen to start walking back to her home. He warned her that the moment her feet entered the city, her young son would die. This tragic sign would prove that all of God's other warnings would also come true.

All Israel would weep for this boy and give him a loving, proper burial. He was the only person in Jeroboam's house who would receive an honorable grave, because God saw true goodness and devotion in his heart. God took the boy early to spare him from the horrors falling on his family.

The Lord announced that He would raise up a new king over Israel who would destroy Jeroboam's entire line. This judgment was not far away; the man who would do it was already alive. Baasha would soon become king and wipe out the royal family.

God warned that Israel would be shaken back and forth like a weak reed blowing in river currents. Eventually, the people would be pulled up from their homeland and scattered far beyond the Euphrates River into exile. This disaster would come because they set up wooden Asherah poles to honor a false Canaanite goddess.

The northern nation of Israel would be handed over to foreign conquerors. This ruin was the direct result of Jeroboam's personal sins and the false religion he forced on the people. Leaders bear heavy responsibility for how they guide others.

Jeroboam's wife turned and traveled back to the beautiful city of Tirzah, where the king had a residence. Just as she stepped across the threshold of the doorway, the child passed away. Everything happened exactly as the prophet had warned.

The royal family buried the boy, and the whole nation mourned for him. This sorrow fulfilled the promise God gave through Ahijah. The fulfillment of this near prediction confirmed that God's broader warnings would also come to pass.

The writer notes that Jeroboam's military battles and daily rule were recorded in the official court records of Israel's kings. Those state archives have been lost over time, but the Bible records the spiritual lessons that matter forever. Earthly success means little if a person leaves God out of their life.

Jeroboam ruled over the northern kingdom for twenty-two years before he died. When his life ended, his son Nadab succeeded him on the throne. Even after all God's warnings, Jeroboam never led the nation back to the true worship of the Lord.

The story turns back to the southern kingdom of Judah, where Solomon's son Rehoboam was reigning. He was forty-one years old when his rule began, and he led the nation from Jerusalem for seventeen years. His mother was Naamah, a woman from the neighboring pagan nation of Ammon.

The people of Judah turned away from God and fell into deep wickedness. Their disloyalty and idol worship provoked the Lord to intense jealousy, just as unfaithfulness wounds a marriage. They practiced even worse sins than earlier generations had committed.

The people built pagan altars on high hills, along with sacred stones and wooden Asherah poles under shady trees. Instead of traveling to worship at the holy temple in Jerusalem, they copied the outdoor shrines of Canaanite religion. Leaving God's true ways opened the door to widespread corruption.

Idol worship in Judah grew so corrupt that male shrine prostitutes were active in the land. The people adopted the vile customs of the pagan nations that God had driven out during Joshua's day. Sin had completely infected their spiritual and moral lives.

In the fifth year of Rehoboam's reign, Pharaoh Shishak of Egypt marched an army against Jerusalem. God allowed this foreign invasion to discipline the nation for forsaking His law. When God's people turn to idols, they lose His divine protection.

Shishak took away the royal riches from the palace and the sacred treasures from God's temple. He also seized the three hundred famous ceremonial shields made of pure gold that Solomon had created. The immense wealth accumulated during years of obedience was lost in a single campaign.

King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace the valuable gold ones that had been stolen. He placed them in the custody of the palace gatekeepers who guarded the royal entrance. The cheaper metal showed how Judah's spiritual glory and earthly honor had faded.

Whenever Rehoboam walked into the temple to worship, the royal guards marched with the bronze shields to make an impressive display. As soon as the king finished, they carried the shields right back to the guardhouse. The ceremony looked grand on the outside, but it could not hide the spiritual decline within.

The rest of Rehoboam's political decisions and public actions were written in the official records of the kings of Judah. Scripture focuses mainly on how faithfully a leader followed the Lord rather than their political achievements. God measures our lives by our devotion to Him.

Tension and border warfare continued between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their lifetimes. Even though God forbade an all-out civil war between brothers, rivalry and fighting never truly stopped. Broken relationships often lead to long-lasting strife.

Rehoboam died and was buried with his royal ancestors in the City of David in Jerusalem. The text repeats that his mother was an Ammonite woman, reminding readers of the foreign pagan roots that influenced his downfall. His son Abijam then became the next king of Judah.
